newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt sees no need for more 97 budget steps.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt sees no need for more 97 budget steps.

text.p: Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi was quoted on Friday as saying he saw no immediate need for additional steps to reduce Italy's 1997 budget deficit in the drive to join Europe's single currency.
But he told La Stampa newspaper that it was vital to tackle structural reform to Italian welfare spending, including on state pensions, in time for the 1998 budget.
"I continue to think that the measures we have adopted (for 1997) are sufficient to meet the objectives" for membership of economic and monetary union (EMU), Ciampi was quoted as saying.

"If unforeseen spending trends emerge we can assess it then," he added. He was echoed by deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni who told reporters on Friday that there was "no need to imagine a third budget" for 1997.

The centre-left government recently drew up an additional mini-budget of revenue-raising measures for 1997 on top of the full budget in a bid to limit the deficit to 3.0 percent of Gross Domestic Product - a key target for EMU entry.

The European Commission forecast on Wednesday that Italy's 1997 deficit would be 3.2 percent of GDP -- outside the three percent ceiling set by the Maastricht Treaty to join the single European currency from its launch in January 1999.
It added that if all recent budget measures were fully effective, Italy might still reach the three percent level, though it forecast a 3.9 percent deficit-to-GDP ratio for 1998.
Ciampi acknowledged that the forecast was a signal that Italy had to move fast on welfare state reform.

"Negotiations on the welfare state cannot be put off any longer," Ciampi was quoted as saying. "A check on the pensions system must be carried out immediately, this year, so that the measures have an effect on 1998 accounts."
Prime Minister Romano Prodi promised on Thursday to introduce structural welfare reform by the beginning of 1998.
"We have said that we will have completed a reform of the welfare state by January 1, 1998 after wide-ranging talks open to everyone," Prodi told a rally in the central town of Lucca.
"By the first of January we will have a structural transformation," he added.
Talks with trades unions over welfare reform are due to start before the middle of May, but agreement between all the various parties will be hard to achieve.
The hard left party Communist Refoundation, which secures Prodi's majority in the lower house of parliament, has already ruled out any cuts in welfare spending.
